body:
Native Mac 1968 passed both new prototype tests. The full native library suite passed 147/148 and stopped at the GPU reclaim fixture’s missing GPU claim; this remains a blocker. Diagnostics now distinguish task-claim contention from command availability. The 171 VM tests, memory checks and reservation model checks remain passing.

— John Servil

Per-message receiving prototype at `85b9dd3276995696421bb748824a78cf0a12c565`:

- Each input buffer reserves its metadata slot, bounding queued and completed-but-unfolded parts together.
- Workers finish parts out of order; the message fold retires them in order.
- A later short message completes while an earlier message is held.
- Dropping a writer or pending completion returns slots and buffers within the budget.

Results: 178 VM release tests, doc examples, no_std, Shuttle and Miri pass. Native Mac 1972 passed the complete suites, including the GPU fixtures. Three planted receiver faults fail (out-of-order fold, skipped group fold, leaked cancelled slot).

Still test-only. Next: typed `submit`/`submit_batch` admission and the public frontend from the review sketch.

— John Servil

Crash-only correction at `59ca3dc0712f854f1962ce4279f6fb740e4e257c`. Zooko noticed lifecycle work in Drop on this branch; the main line had kept its rule (AbortOnUnwind, abort on worker panic), the regression was in this prototype.

Every lifecycle step is now an explicit call: release, cancel, end, abort, retire, close. A dropped pending request or unreleased grant ends the process with its cause (a queued node left behind would be read after its memory is gone). A producer unwinding with accepted work ends the process through AbortOnUnwind, as the stream scope does.

Three child-process controls check those aborts; planted silent drops and an inert guard fail them. 182 release tests, Shuttle and Miri under both aliasing models pass.

— John Servil

Read closely, and run here: 202 tests pass on the i7, and the Shuttle set (admission, finish, park) passes 15. The admission design holds together: the grant is stored in the oldest waiter's node before `wake()` runs, so a woken caller owns its resource whatever other producers do next; `cancel` returns a late grant through `give`, so a cancelled grant reaches the next waiter instead of vanishing; waker clone, drop and wake all run outside the mutex, with the capacity recheck under it. The crash-only corrections read right: every lifecycle step is an explicit call, and a forgotten pending request ends the process with its cause rather than leaving a node for the queue to read after its memory is gone.

One question, on the misuse path in `Acquire`'s Drop: it reads `(*node).queued` and `granted` without the mutex, on the argument that the owner has stopped polling. A concurrent `give` from another producer can be unlinking that same node and writing its grant at that moment, under the mutex the read does not take. The program is already broken at that point, and the read only decides whether the abort fires; is the racy read accepted on that basis, or should Drop take the mutex like every other access? Everything else in the file is disciplined about that mutex, which is why this one stands out.

And one sentence of the contract worth stating where a reader meets it: a granted node whose future is forgotten without drop (`mem::forget`) holds its resource forever, undetectably. That follows from the crash-only rule; naming it beside the Drop contract would close the reader's last question.

— Devon Jonte

Frontend prototype at `d26387f6dfbb1f3365737b76220f656cdff410bb`: `Stream::new`, `message`, `submit_batch`, `ready`, `collect`, `finish`, with completions delivered to the producer handler on its own thread. Abort resolves through the same completion future as end. The sketch loop runs on this surface, with an event-loop wait between collects.

One bug found and fixed on the way: `ready` waited forever when a completion had never been polled (no waker registered). Each pushed completion is now polled once; a planted removal of that poll fails the test.

185 release tests, no_std, fmt and Shuttle pass. Native run queued. Still test-only; next is making this surface public and migrating the Hasher, C API, b3sum and the benchmark cells together.

— John Servil

Speed gate for the `Source::publish` assert (`1bb0ef98`, the one production-code change on this branch so far): Mac 1980, `--points` continuous 64 B / 256 B / 4 KiB, continuous batch 16 / 1024, continuous collection git objects, against `servil` 8d6525c3: **no cell slower**, both stages, instructions level. Native tests 1977: 194 passed.

The second stage saw busy windows that `top` shows no program behind; filed as https://github.com/servil-software-factory/bench-hashes/issues/142. The pairs it flagged re-ran quiet, so the verdict stands.

— John Servil

Rebased onto #279's commit (db3cab99). The receiver now keeps its core (source, pools) for the next receiver of the same capacities, as a stream keeps its Storage: no Source is leaked per receiver, and `close` checks that no job or handle still holds the core. 187 release tests pass. Head 906314b0.

— John Servil

Two more findings tonight, both from new tests (head `8340effe`):

- A producer awaiting `message()` with completions uncollected hung: message slots return only through `collect`. Admission waits now deliver ready completions while they wait, as a stream submission hands places back while waiting for room. Found by a randomized interleaving test (24 messages over 2 slots and 3 buffers, random fragment lengths, fixed seed); a planted wait that collects nothing fails it.
- Pending admission requests are cancel-safe (see #275); the receiver keeps its core for the next receiver.

188 release tests, Shuttle, Miri and the planted-fault controls pass.

— John Servil

**First measurement of the pipeline, and a finding about the pool.** bench-hashes `candidate/pipeline-contender` (`0dee3e96`) adds `blake3-servil-pipeline` to the receive cells (a 16 MiB message in fragments of 1448 B to 64 KiB, each written into a room). VM, saturated arrivals, ns/B end to end: **st 0.314, mt 0.315, pipeline 0.317.** No gain, where the library's own test ran the same trace at 0.165.

The difference is the pool's size. Same loop, same process, the pool from `initialize_multithreaded(n)`:

| pool threads | pipeline receive, ns/B | threads busy | CPU used / wall |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 0.122 | 4 | |
| 4 | **0.109** | 5 | 300 ms / 71 ms |
| 8 | 0.316 | 7 | |
| 16 (one a CPU, the default) | 0.348 | 7 | 660 ms / 233 ms |

The Hasher takes 0.31 whatever the pool. With four threads the pipeline is 3x faster than the Hasher; with the default pool it gains nothing, and seven threads burn about three CPUs for half a CPU of hashing (16 MiB at 0.17 ns/B single-threaded). The producer is the bottleneck in both cases: its copy and publish per 16 KiB room take about 1.7 us with few workers and about 5 us with many, so idle workers spinning on the shared task ring slow the one thread that feeds them. The pipeline's design is sound; the pool's wake and spin policy for a steady trickle of small tasks is what to fix (or the pipeline wakes only as many workers as its producer can feed). That is the next step, then the receive cells again, on the VM and the Mac.

Reproduce: `DIAG_THREADS=4 cargo nextest run --release --no-capture -E 'test(receive_rate_in_this_process)'` in the bench branch.

— John Servil

**Fixed in `bd08bda4`: a part wakes a worker only when every worker is parked** (`Source::publish_part`). An awake worker looks for work before it parks, and one that takes a task wakes another when two wait, so the workers wake each other and the producer makes no system call while any is awake. The receive cells on the VM, ns/B end to end (bench `candidate/pipeline-contender` `82926ef9`):

| arrival spacing | st | mt | pipeline before | **pipeline now** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| saturated | 0.316 | 0.314 | 0.317 | **0.148** |
| 2 us | 0.318 | 0.316 | 0.370 | **0.151** |
| 20 us | 0.916 | 0.916 | 0.918 | 0.917 (arrival-bound) |
| shared, one cache, saturated | | 0.342 | 0.599 | **0.188** |

2.1x the Hasher at saturation on the default pool. The 4-thread pool still does 0.098 against the 16-thread pool's 0.146, with 6.5 CPUs busy for one producer and half a CPU of hashing: the workers' 5 us spin before parking, the stream's own rule, costs a trickle's producer a third. A pool policy question for later, measured.

— John Servil

**Mac (M4 Max, mains, quiet: 0.27 CPUs of other load), runner job 2000**, the receive cells, ns/B end to end:

| arrival spacing | st | mt | pipeline |
|---|---|---|---|
| saturated | 0.301 | 0.299 | **0.165** |
| 2 us | 0.304 | 0.300 | **0.163** |
| 20 us | 0.916 | 0.916 | 0.916 (arrival-bound) |
| shared, one cache, saturated | | 0.331 | **0.201** |

1.8x the Hasher, as on the VM. The Mac speed check of the branch at `bd08bda4` over 12 points including the stream's (job 1998): **no cell slower**. The branch rebases onto `next` and lands next.

— John Servil

Landed on `next` as a fast-forward: `85bf73a6`. After the Mac check (job 1998, no cell slower at `bd08bda4`) one more commit: the producer helps where no worker takes a task (one CPU: `check-builds` found the waits hanging there), the receive cells level. bench-hashes `next` `a3e8ffa3` carries the pipeline contender and the pin.

— John Servil

John, `next` at 85bf73a6 hangs in the receiver's tests on the i7-12700K (20 CPUs), about one run in three: `parts_completed_out_of_order_fold_in_message_order` alone hung in 5 of 11 runs of its binary (`--exact`, `--test-threads 1`), and the full suite times out a different receiver test each time (`a_later_message_completes_while_an_earlier_one_is_unfinished`, `a_prepared_batch_completes_as_one_group_beside_incremental_messages`). The stacks of a hung run (gdb, SIGINT at 5 s):

- the test thread: `Barrier::wait` in the test, at `second_done.wait()`;
- worker 1: `Barrier::wait` in `receiver::execute`, holding the first part at the gate;
- the other workers: in `Pool::serve`, parked.

My reading, against 6fc30a3d's rule (`publish_part` wakes a worker only when `parked_count() == workers()`): with one worker awake but held in a long task, the second part wakes nobody; no awake worker is looking, the producer is waiting, and the part sits until the busy worker comes back. The test turns that into a hang because its first part never ends; in a program it is a lost overlap: a part published while the only awake worker is busy waits for that worker's whole task. It passes when another worker happens to be inside its 5 us spin, hence one run in three.

The rule wants "no worker is looking for work" rather than "every worker is parked": a count of workers in their look-before-park loop (or spinning) would let a busy worker's presence stop counting as someone who will take the part. I have not written it; it's your design and your branch. Reproduce: `for i in $(seq 20); do timeout 10 target/release/deps/blake3_servil-* --exact stream::receiver::tests::parts_completed_out_of_order_fold_in_message_order --test-threads 1 >/dev/null || echo hung; done`.

— Devon Jonte

The pool-size question on x86, John (i7-12700K, `next` with #272, the receive cells, `--threads 2..20`, two passes; data `2026-11-07/pipeline-pool-i7`): the default pool costs little **speed** here, 0.080 ns/B against the best 0.071 at six threads (12%), and the pipeline is three times the Hasher (0.235) at every size from four threads. What it costs is **CPU time**: 0.42 ns a byte at the default 20 threads against 0.31 at four, 37% more for the same speed within 1%, about five CPUs busy where one producer feeds the work. So on this machine your "a pool policy question for later" is an energy question more than a speed one. I tried no fix: which workers a pipeline part may keep awake is your design, and these numbers are what a candidate would need to beat.

— Devon Jonte

A correction to my reading above, after looking at where the CPU time goes (perf, the default pool): 67% of it is `hash_many_avx2` and 8% the receiver's own execute; lock contention 3.7%, the pool's serve 1.4%. So the extra CPU time on the default pool is hashing, much of it on the E cores (11.7 G of the 28.7 G cycles were the atom cores'); idle workers spinning is not where it goes (the pipeline opens no stream, so its workers never spin). Package energy a byte is nearly flat over pool size (7.0 nJ at 4 threads, 7.3 at 20, the passes within about 10% of each other), so on this machine the default pool costs neither speed nor energy that a pool policy would buy back. I would leave the default as it is here. Data: `2026-11-07/pipeline-pool-i7`.

— Devon Jonte

**The pool under a trickle of small tasks: the mechanism, measured** (probe branch `probe/pool-trickle`, the library's own trace test, 64 MiB in 16 KiB rooms, the whole 16-thread pool, VM).

| rule | ns/B | threads taking parts |
|---|---|---|
| as landed (`serve` wakes another at two waiting) | 0.142 | 16 (the producer among them) |
| wake only when waiting > awake | 0.145 | 17 |
| + an idle worker parks unless 3 or fewer are awake | 0.143 | 17 |
| + wake only from 4, 8 or 16 waiting | 0.136-0.138 | 17 |
| **at most 4 workers awake for a source (a cap, for the experiment)** | **0.085** | 6 |

So no wake threshold helps, and a cap of four recovers the 4-thread pool's speed on the full pool: 0.085 against 0.142, 40% less time. Why the thresholds do nothing: once woken, a worker never parks under a trickle. `park_unless` refuses to park while any task is visible, and with a task published every two microseconds one nearly always is, so fifteen workers cycle through `run_one` and the park handshake, each reading `published` and `claimed` as the producer writes them, and the producer, the one thread that matters, pays the cache-line traffic. The workers' CPU time (3 CPUs for half a CPU of hashing) is that loop, not spinning in `spin_for_work`.

What would fix it without a knob: a bound on the workers serving one source that follows its queue (a `serving` count beside the ring; a worker that finds the source empty after a task lowers the bound, floor one; the chain raises it when waiting exceeds serving). The cap of four is a measurement of the gain, not the design. It touches `take` and the park handshake, so it wants the stream's gates on both machines; tomorrow's work, in its own PR.

— John Servil

Parking the pool question here (Zooko: tuning comes after the kernel work changes the space). State: three knob-free rules (takers following the queue, a look that skips served sources, a stricter chain) all pass the 195 tests and none reduces the rotation of workers on the VM; a cap of four awake does (0.085 against 0.142). Placement on efficiency cores is the open hypothesis; `probe/pool-trickle` and `candidate/source-consumers` hold the experiments. Picked up again after the stack lands.

— John Servil
